reason: Pioneer 10's groundbreaking mission through the asteroid belt and Jupiter's lethal radiation is supported by multiple independent sources.
story: In March 1972, NASA launched Pioneer 10 on a daring 21-month mission to Jupiter. Blasting off atop an Atlas-Centaur rocket, it became the fastest human-made object in history, exceeding 32,000 miles per hour. Pioneer 10 braved unprecedented dangers, becoming the first spacecraft to enter and successfully cross the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Arriving at Jupiter in December 1973, it endured radiation ten thousand times stronger than Earth's radiation belts. The intense radiation fried onboard systems and triggered false electronic commands, but Pioneer 10 survived to capture the very first close-up images of Jupiter's Great Red Spot. The probe didn't stop there. In 1983, it became the first craft to cross Neptune's orbit into the outer solar system. Carrying an iconic golden plaque depicting humanity for potential alien civilizations, Pioneer 10 sent its last faint signal to Earth in January 2003. Today, it quietly drifts towards the star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus.
angle: Pioneer 10 survived Jupiter's radiation belts—10,000 times stronger than Earth's—which triggered false electronic commands, to return the first close-up photos of the Great Red Spot.

claims.claim: Pioneer 10 launched in March 1972 aboard an Atlas-Centaur rocket.
At launch, Pioneer 10 reached a speed over 32,000 mph (51,600 km/h), making it the fastest human-made object at the time.
Pioneer 10 was originally designed for a 21-month mission to explore Jupiter.
In July 1972, Pioneer 10 became the first spacecraft to enter and traverse the main asteroid belt.
Pioneer 10 successfully emerged on the far side of the asteroid belt in February 1973.
Pioneer 10 returned the first close-up images of Jupiter and its Great Red Spot.
Intense Jovian electron radiation triggered false electronic commands aboard Pioneer 10 during its flyby.
On June 13, 1983, Pioneer 10 became the first human-made object to pass beyond the orbit of Neptune.
On February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 surpassed Pioneer 10 as the most distant human-made object from Earth.
Pioneer 10 transmitted its final signal back to Earth on January 23, 2003.
A final attempt to contact Pioneer 10 was made on March 4, 2006, but received no response.
Pioneer 10 carries a gold-anodized aluminum plaque with drawings of a human man and woman for intelligent extraterrestrial life.
Pioneer 10 is traveling out of the solar system in the direction of the constellation Taurus toward the red star Aldebaran.
The Pioneer anomaly, an unexpected slight deceleration of the probe, was ultimately explained by uneven heat radiation from the spacecraft.
A US 10-cent commemorative postage stamp honoring Pioneer 10 was issued in Mountain View, California, on February 28, 1975.

disputed: The number of RTGs onboard is reported as four by S1 and two SNAP-19 units by S2; script should refer generally to its nuclear SNAP-19 RTG power supply without specifying total module count.
The exact date of closest approach to Jupiter is reported as Dec 3, 1973 in S1, Dec 4 (02:26 UT) in S2, and Dec 2 in S6; script should use 'early December 1973'.
The exact closest approach distance varies between 132,252 km (82,178 mi) in S1 and 81,000 miles (130,354 km) in S2 and S6; script should state 'about 81,000 miles'.
